title: AI's Impact on Legal Education: Preparing Future Lawyers for a Tech-Driven World — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Everyday usability: Better formats do not prove accuracy

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source accepts the need to move beyond static doctrinal education toward practical technology use, human skills and lifelong learning. It materially develops the cluster by applying the innovator’s-dilemma framework to law schools and proposing concrete questions and a checklist through which applicants can assess institutional readiness.
qs: The world is changing too quickly to have three static years of your life prepare you for the rest of your profession.

While you were talking, I was thinking: yeah, some of the things I would want to learn right now are leadership, change management, creativity, and collaborative work arrangements with unusual partners.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source accepts the engagement-first proposition and develops it through a concrete institutional role for law-school leaders: combining accreditation compliance with AI-enabled work on legal-system problems and collaborating across organisations to change legal education. It presents this as an agenda rather than evidence of educational outcomes.
qs: It would be a really exciting time to be a creative dean who could figure out how to do all the things that the accreditor says you should do — I understand that — but also aim talented law students with these really powerful tools at some of the biggest problems in the legal system.

There's so much to dig into here, and we can learn a little bit more about some of the work that we're doing at the AAA to partner with Suffolk and others right now to drive change in legal education.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that AI requires institutional redesign rather than mere tool adoption and extends the cluster with a concrete legal-education pathway: expose students early to unmet legal need, then equip them to apply AI creatively to those problems. It also identifies accreditation constraints and the historic division between academic and workplace training, while offering proposals rather than measured educational outcomes.
qs: But you've heard me say this even before generative AI: I would have law students, before they sit in the classroom and read appellate cases, spend the first few weeks in state courtrooms where people are trying to manage their justice problems — most of whom are managing them without lawyers, because most people in the US can't afford lawyers.

It excites me to think about giving incoming law students the power to use those tools, and the information about what they might use them for, that I think could really change some of the biggest problems in the profession.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI is changing legal practice and extends the cluster’s work-redesign thesis to lawyer preparation, examining whether law schools are adapting curricula and student experiences. Its contribution is cautious: the 29-school response pool cannot establish widespread curricular redesign, and claims about institutional inaction remain speculative.
qs: We decided that one of the things our subcommittee could offer was just to try and figure out the state of where law schools are in thinking about how to approach the fact that generative AI is changing the practice of law, the business of law, and sort of to see who's doing what about it.
Obviously that is a very small number, and it means there's no way to take the survey results as representative of what's happening — because who knows what's happening in the rest of them.

st.t: AI competition: Distribution and habits rival capability
st.an: Leonard’s firsthand trial supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between impressive output and validated reliability. NotebookLM sounded strikingly human, yet generated a false implication that the newly created podcast had a prior history; the anecdote does not test legal accuracy or educational effectiveness.
qs: But after a few minutes, it will create a podcast that sounds like two people, and it really sounds human.

These two people started it, and they said, "You know, we talk a lot about AI on this show" — like this show that didn't exist until we hit "Podcast." "And this week, we're going to do a deep dive into an industry that is really primed for impact from AI: the legal profession.

st.t: Everyday usability: Better formats do not prove accuracy
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by presenting conversational audio as a convenient supplement to eventual reading, while grounding accuracy claims in a single informal test that also revealed terminology problems. Its reported and planned uses are experiential rather than systematic evidence of accuracy, learning outcomes or institutional readiness.
qs: Like we talked about, they will read the documents eventually, but it really helps them understand what's in them through conversation.
There were a couple places where it used terminology that maybe wasn't perfect — like, I think it said "practice focus" instead of "practice areas" or something like that.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports practitioner-led experimentation before technological certainty by proposing AI-assisted legal-learning uses while treating claimed benefits as anecdotal rather than established. Its warning about AI washing reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on reliability and informed implementation rather than uncritical adoption.
qs: I also thought — to segue into our topic for today of legal education — what a different world it would have been if I could have uploaded a Torts case to a podcast and then listened to people talk about it, as well as studying and briefing it the old-fashioned way.
It's companies overstating or over-exaggerating the capabilities or use of artificial intelligence in their products.

kp.k: AI washing complicates lawyers' technology purchasing
kp.d: Leonard defines AI washing as overstating products' AI capabilities or use. She reports that existing, sometimes non-generative AI tools are being repackaged with generative AI claims, leaving some legal consumers disappointed. She identifies FTC activity involving DoNotPay as an example of consumer protection intervention and expects further attention; these are her reported observations, not systematic purchasing evidence.
qs: It's companies overstating or over-exaggerating the capabilities or use of artificial intelligence in their products.
And I've heard a lot of disappointed consumers in the legal industry who were unaware of the limitations of some of the products that are being pitched to them.
I've seen that there are some FTC efforts to sort of curb AI washing — the DoNotPay "robot lawyer" is one of the targets of some of that activity.

kp.k: Larger context windows expand document-processing capacity
kp.d: McCormack describes context windows as a model's working memory. She reports that some newer models have windows of up to 100,000 or 200,000 tokens, which she has been told correspond to up to roughly 300 pages in a single prompt, and anticipates further growth. Her page conversion and expectations are qualified rather than presented as tested performance findings.
qs: And it's the large language model's working memory, meaning the amount of information it can take in and consider at once when making a particular decision or giving a particular answer.

Some of the newer models right now have context windows of up to 100,000 or 200,000 tokens, which I am told translates to being able to comprehend up to, I guess, 300 pages of text in a single prompt.

kp.k: Headshot generation illustrates adjacent professional-service disruption
kp.d: McCormack recounts a colleague uploading 10 selfies to InstaHeadshots and receiving 100 professional headshots, with a reported cost of about $65 and generation time of about 10 seconds. She says AAA subsequently bought licenses for public-facing employees. Leonard contrasts this with her own conventional photography costs and preparation, calling it another disrupted industry. This is an anecdotal example outside legal work, not measured evidence of market displacement.
qs: So eventually she found 10 selfies and uploaded them all, and then it produced 100 professional headshots.
And I think the cost was like $65, and it did it in about 10 seconds.
we went ahead and just bought a bunch of licenses and offered them to any employees who are public-facing.
And I think my immediate reaction was, there's another industry disrupted, just for the reasons you're saying.

kp.k: AI audio supports document comprehension and varied learning
kp.d: Leonard describes testing Notebook LM by converting a presentation outline into a synthetic conversational podcast. She judged its expansions nuanced and accurate, while noting minor terminology problems. She reports friends listening to legal-document discussions during commutes before eventually reading the documents, and suggests similar supplementary uses for law students and neurodiverse learners. These are personal experiences and proposed educational benefits, not evaluated learning outcomes.
qs: And it went through all the things in our outline, and it expanded on the bullet points in ways that were really, really nuanced and accurate.
Like we talked about, they will read the documents eventually, but it really helps them understand what's in them through conversation.
So I think it also opens up opportunities for neurodiverse learners and for people who want to hear discussions about the material, maybe before going to class.

kp.k: Survey cannot establish widespread law-school AI preparedness
kp.d: McCormack says an ABA Task Force on AI and Law legal-education subcommittee surveyed almost 200 accredited law schools, but only 29 completed and returned the survey. She explicitly rejects treating the responses as representative. Her suggestion that nonrespondents likely had little activity is a guess. Leonard says optimistic coverage led some law firms she visited to assume schools were preparing students adequately. The supplied transcript omits the promised detailed survey findings, so it supports no further adoption statistics.
qs: So we sent out a survey — as one does — to the almost 200 law schools that are accredited across the country
only 29 schools completed the survey and responded to it.
Obviously that is a very small number, and it means there's no way to take the survey results as representative of what's happening — because who knows what's happening in the rest of them.
My guess, though, is that the rest of the law schools likely didn't have a lot of answers to the questions because they just weren't doing anything yet
their takeaway has been like, "We have confidence that the law schools are already responding and preparing students for a world transformed by generative AI."

kp.k: Accreditation can enable and constrain educational adaptation
kp.d: McCormack reports appointing a committee of accreditation Council members to examine AI's implications for the accreditor and how it might encourage law-school responses, led by Colorado Supreme Court Justice Melissa Hart. She later qualifies her reform proposals by stressing that accreditation already requires schools to do many specific things. No completed committee recommendations or new accreditation requirements are reported.
qs: one of my last acts as Chair of the Section on Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar was to appoint a committee of Council members to take a look at what AI should mean to the accreditor
And Justice Melissa Hart from the Colorado Supreme Court is leading that task force
law schools don't have unfettered freedom to just do whatever they want — because the accreditor requires them to do an awful lot of specific things

kp.d: Applying the innovator's dilemma framework, Leonard describes modern law schools as historically innovative institutions that separated theoretical formation from practical training supplied by firms under the Cravath model. She argues that scholarship-centered faculty incentives and the separation of employment-focused administrators from curriculum-setting tenured faculty now inhibit adaptation to practice. She qualifies the analogy by recognizing clinical and legal-writing reforms and law schools' distinctive market pressures.
qs: they would be employed by law firms, who would then actually teach them the practical skills they needed to have.
We've had the rise of clinical programs, we've had the rise of legal writing as a core part of training new law students to prepare for entering practice.

Not much of that conversation — explicitly tied to employment outcomes — happens in the tenured faculty arena, even though those are the stakeholders who make the decisions about what goes into the core curriculum.
So I think that that divide is something that really holds law schools back in some ways from being responsive to the changing demands of practice.

kp.k: Appellate-centered teaching may mismatch graduates' eventual work
kp.d: Leonard reports Alice Armitage's critique that the required first year emphasizes appellate cases and oral argument despite most students not pursuing appellate careers. Leonard places this within her broader argument that inherited educational structures impede rapid responses to changing practice; it is an attributed critique, not an empirical career-outcome finding.
qs: Alice has talked about how the first year in particular — which is the year when everything is required and consistent across the board — is really designed to produce appellate lawyers in the way that we teach appellate case law and the way that we focus on oral argument, when most people are not going to pursue careers in appellate law.

kp.k: AI preparedness could reorder law-school competition
kp.d: McCormack argues that ranking systems inhibit innovation and speculates that students investing in three years of education may increasingly prioritize preparation for technological change over traditional U.S. News metrics. She sees a possible opportunity for schools such as Suffolk to leapfrog higher-ranked institutions. Leonard notes schools' retreat from rankings but explicitly guesses, partly from prospective-student conversations, that students still rely on them because no alternative selection framework exists.
qs: the way that ranking system inhibits innovation.

At least it feels possible to me that if you're thinking about spending a whole lot of money on three years of education for a profession that's changing very quickly right now, you're probably going to want to pay attention to something other than what U.S. News & World Report says
I do think there are opportunities for the Suffolk Law Schools of the world to leapfrog a lot of other law schools
because there's currently not another framework to use to select law schools, prospective students continue to use the U.S. News rankings right now to make decisions.

kp.k: Applicants should investigate actual technology preparation
kp.d: McCormack recommends going beyond rankings and marketing by questioning relevant administrators about AI-related learning and professional development. Leonard advises examining a school's history of technology integration, whether practical technology instruction is core or elective, and whether tenured faculty teach technology use rather than merely technology law. She also recommends work experience before law school to clarify career fit and observe how lawyers' work evolves over the next few years.
qs: I think this is a really important moment to look far beyond both the rankings and even the marketing materials that schools are producing about what their curriculum does and doesn't do.
Is that integrated into the core curriculum, or are they only electives that are offered?
Do you have tenured faculty members who focus on not just the substance of technology law, but actually how to use technology in practice?

if you're just graduating undergrad, I definitely recommend taking a couple of years to work, to figure out what you actually enjoy doing and whether that aligns with what lawyers actually do on the ground day to day.

kp.k: Lifelong learning and human skills need greater emphasis
kp.d: Leonard argues that three years of static education cannot prepare lawyers for a rapidly changing career and recommends teaching metacognition and continuing skill development beyond conventional annual CLE. McCormack identifies leadership, change management, creativity, and collaboration with unusual partners as increasingly important. She notes that these skills are not generally part of the traditional curriculum but can potentially be taught within existing subjects through changed pedagogy.
qs: The world is changing too quickly to have three static years of your life prepare you for the rest of your profession.
So how does your school help me understand how I learn as a lawyer, and what skills I'll need to continually develop beyond the typical CLE every year, in a rapidly changing world?
some of the things I would want to learn right now are leadership, change management, creativity, and collaborative work arrangements with unusual partners.
I'm not saying you can't teach them within some of the traditional curriculum — I think you can; it just depends on how you're teaching that traditional curriculum.

kp.k: Early justice-gap exposure could guide AI-enabled student innovation
kp.d: McCormack proposes that incoming students spend their first few weeks observing state courtrooms before studying appellate cases, encountering people managing justice problems without lawyers. She argues that this would orient students' creativity toward unmet legal need, and that AI supplies new tools for addressing those problems. This is a proposed educational and access-to-justice intervention, qualified by accreditation constraints, not evidence that student AI projects have already reduced the justice gap.
qs: I would have law students, before they sit in the classroom and read appellate cases, spend the first few weeks in state courtrooms where people are trying to manage their justice problems — most of whom are managing them without lawyers, because most people in the US can't afford lawyers.
And I now think that this technology just gives them new tools to think about how to solve those problems.

It excites me to think about giving incoming law students the power to use those tools, and the information about what they might use them for, that I think could really change some of the biggest problems in the profession.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack describe AI-enabled changes in legal learning and practice, predict competitive opportunities for technology-oriented law schools, and propose using AI education to address unmet legal need.
pts.d: 1. Jen Leonard claims that legal-product marketing increasingly overstates generative-AI capabilities or repackages older AI tools, disappointing some legal-industry buyers; she expects more consumer-protection activity. 2. Leonard reports that Notebook LM can turn legal material into conversational audio that helps users understand documents before reading them. She predicts supplementary learning opportunities for law students, including neurodiverse learners. 3. Bridget McCormack describes generative AI as changing legal practice and the business of law, but both speakers caution that law schools' readiness cannot be inferred from a small ABA survey. McCormack guesses that many nonresponding schools had not yet begun responding; Leonard reports that optimistic coverage has given some law firms unwarranted confidence in graduate preparation. 4. Leonard argues that curriculum governance, scholarship-oriented incentives, and the separation between faculty decision-making and employment-focused offices impede rapid adaptation to practice changes. McCormack predicts that AI-related preparation could become a competitive differentiator, allowing schools such as Suffolk to leapfrog traditionally higher-ranked institutions in prospective students' estimation. 5. Leonard argues that accelerating change makes three years of static education insufficient for a whole career, increasing the importance of metacognition and lifelong learning. McCormack identifies leadership, change management, creativity, and collaboration as increasingly important human skills. 6. McCormack proposes combining early exposure to unmet civil legal need with access to AI tools so creative students can help solve legal-system problems. This is a possibility and educational prescription, not a reported access-to-justice outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The episode relies primarily on professional experience, product-use anecdotes, and explicitly qualified speculation; its principal empirical reference is an ABA survey with only 29 respondents.
pts.d: 1. For AI washing, Leonard cites reports she has heard from disappointed legal-industry consumers and FTC activity involving DoNotPay; she supplies no quantified prevalence or detailed enforcement findings. 2. For conversational audio, Leonard describes testing Notebook LM with a colleague using their generative-AI presentation outline. She judged the expansion nuanced and accurate, with minor terminology issues, and relays friends' accounts of listening to legal documents. No measured learning outcomes, legal-document accuracy study, or neurodiverse-learner results are offered. 3. McCormack participated in the ABA legal-education subcommittee that surveyed almost 200 accredited law schools, of which 29 responded. She explicitly says these responses are not representative. The supplied transcript omits substantive survey findings after introducing them; it does not support extracting course-adoption percentages or other missing results. The explanation for nonresponse is McCormack's guess, not a survey finding. Leonard's account of law-firm confidence derives from her visits with firms. 4. The curriculum and competition arguments draw on both speakers' legal-education experience, institutional reasoning, and the innovator's-dilemma framework. Leonard explicitly characterizes her account of prospective students' continued reliance on rankings as a guess informed by a few conversations. No enrollment, ranking, or employment-outcome data substantiate the predicted competitive shift. 5. The lifelong-learning and human-skills claims are professional judgments rather than measured findings. 6. The proposed access-to-justice benefits are aspirational, with no demonstrated AI intervention or outcome data supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion distinguishes reported uses in 2024 from conditional changes over the next several years and longer-term educational possibilities.
pts.d: 1. Leonard describes AI washing as already occurring and expects continued attention as consumer-protection agencies and groups become involved; no deadline is given. 2. Notebook LM use is contemporaneous with the episode. Its educational application is prospective and supplementary: Leonard explicitly says her friends will still read the underlying documents and imagines audio alongside conventional studying and briefing. 3. The ABA survey concerns preparedness earlier in 2024. Both speakers emphasize its low response rate; neither establishes the actual readiness of nonresponding institutions. 4. McCormack frames disruption of law-school choice as possible rather than certain, connecting it to students investing in three years of education. She suggests older ranking metrics will be less relevant in three, five, or ten years. The opportunity depends on students valuing preparation for technology-driven practice and schools adapting their offerings. Leonard also advises prospective students to observe how professional life develops over the next three to five years. 5. Lifelong learning is presented as a current need extending beyond graduation; human-skills instruction need not require entirely new courses, because McCormack says it can occur within traditional curricula depending on teaching methods. 6. The access-to-justice proposal has no specified delivery date and requires students to understand real justice problems, obtain useful tools, and work within accreditation constraints. McCormack explicitly notes that her proposal for early courtroom exposure predates generative AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected groups are prospective and current law students, law schools and their faculty, hiring law firms, legal-tool buyers, and people unable to obtain civil legal assistance.
pts.d: 1. Lawyers and legal-industry software buyers face a gap between marketed and actual product capabilities; vendors face anticipated consumer-protection scrutiny. 2. Practitioners can use conversational audio to familiarize themselves with documents during commuting time. Law students, particularly those who benefit from auditory discussion or neurodiverse learning options, may gain additional ways to engage with course material. These examples describe augmentation, not replacing lawyers or relying directly on AI-generated legal advice. 3. Hiring law firms may incorrectly assume that graduates are already being prepared for generative-AI-enabled practice. Law-school administrators, faculty, and the accreditor face decisions about curriculum and professional readiness. 4. Prospective students face expensive educational choices and potentially changing career requirements. Technology-oriented schools may attract interest relative to institutions favored by established rankings; incumbent schools face pressure to demonstrate actual preparation beyond marketing claims. 5. Students and practicing lawyers face continuing skill-development needs, while schools are urged to teach learning strategies and human capabilities as well as substantive law and technology use. 6. Unrepresented people facing civil justice problems are the intended beneficiaries of McCormack's proposal to direct AI-equipped students toward unmet legal need. Students and innovative deans are positioned as possible contributors, not as providers of an already demonstrated solution.
